top_level_objectives: Understand how electron pairs around a central atom arrange to minimize repulsion
Apply VSEPR theory to predict the three-dimensional geometry of covalent molecules
Identify the five fundamental electron-domain geometries and their characteristics
Explain how lone pairs modify molecular geometry relative to electron-domain geometry
Recognize that lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, causing bond-angle deviations

scenes.scene_name: Lewis Structure Review and Electron Domain Identification
scenes.brief_purpose: Establish foundational understanding of Lewis structures and introduce the concept of electron domains as the basis for VSEPR predictions
key_visuals: Lewis structures of simple molecules (CH₄, NH₃, H₂O, CO₂)
Highlighted electron domains around central atoms
Color-coded bonding pairs and lone pairs
student_actions: Examine Lewis structures for given molecules
Count total electron domains (bonding + lone pairs) around the central atom
Identify which domains are bonding pairs and which are lone pairs

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the concept of electron-domain geometry by exploring the simplest case where electron domains arrange in a line to minimize repulsion
key_visuals: Central atom with two electron domains extending outward
Repulsion vectors pushing domains apart to 180° angles
3D model showing linear arrangement
Example molecule: CO₂
student_actions: Manipulate two electron domains around a central atom and observe them settle into linear arrangement
Measure or confirm the 180° bond angle
Compare the predicted linear geometry to the structure of CO₂

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how three electron domains arrange in a plane with 120° separation to minimize repulsion
key_visuals: Central atom with three electron domains
Repulsion vectors and resulting planar orientation
3D model in a triangular plane
Example molecule: BF₃
student_actions: Manipulate three electron domains and watch them settle into trigonal planar geometry
Confirm 120° bond angles
Identify BF₃ as a real example and note that molecular geometry equals electron-domain geometry when no lone pairs are present

scenes.scene_name: Electron Domain Geometry: Tetrahedral and Octahedral
scenes.brief_purpose: Explore the two most common electron-domain geometries for organic and coordination chemistry, showing how four and six domains arrange in 3D space
key_visuals: Tetrahedral arrangement with four domains at ~109.5° angles
Octahedral arrangement with six domains at 90° angles
3D models showing spatial orientation
Example molecules: CH₄ (tetrahedral), SF₆ (octahedral)
student_actions: Manipulate four domains to see tetrahedral geometry form
Manipulate six domains to see octahedral geometry form
Measure or verify approximate bond angles in each
Match predicted geometries to real molecules (methane and sulfur hexafluoride)

scenes.scene_name: Lone Pairs Modify Molecular Geometry: Water and Ammonia
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate that lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, causing deviations from idealized bond angles and different molecular geometries
key_visuals: Water: tetrahedral electron-domain geometry with 2 lone pairs, showing lone pairs occupying larger angular regions
Bond angle of ~104.5° in water versus idealized 109.5° in methane
Ammonia: tetrahedral electron-domain geometry with 1 lone pair, showing trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry
Repulsion strength comparison (lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair)
student_actions: Start with tetrahedral arrangement (4 electron domains)
Add lone pairs and observe molecular geometry shift to bent (water) or trigonal pyramidal (ammonia)
Compare bond angles in water versus methane
Explain qualitatively why lone pairs push bonding pairs closer together

scenes.scene_name: Trigonal Bipyramidal Geometry and Lone Pair Effects
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the 5-electron-domain geometry and show how lone pair placement in equatorial positions creates seesaw and T-shaped geometries
key_visuals: Five domains arranged with three in equatorial plane and two axial
Equatorial positions highlighted as lower-repulsion sites for lone pairs
Seesaw geometry (4 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair)
T-shaped geometry (3 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs)
Example molecules: SF₄ (seesaw), XeF₃⁺ or similar (T-shaped)
student_actions: Manipulate five electron domains to identify trigonal bipyramidal geometry
Add one lone pair in equatorial position and observe seesaw molecular geometry
Add two lone pairs in equatorial positions and observe T-shaped geometry
Recognize why lone pairs prefer equatorial sites (reduced repulsion from 2 rather than 3 neighbors)

scenes.scene_name: Octahedral Geometry and Square Planar Arrangement
scenes.brief_purpose: Examine how six electron domains arrange octahedrally and how lone pairs in specific positions produce square planar molecular geometry
key_visuals: Six domains in octahedral arrangement (four equatorial, two axial)
Lone pair placement in axial positions (trans arrangement)
Square planar molecular geometry resulting from 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs
Example molecule: XeF₄
student_actions: Confirm octahedral electron-domain geometry with six domains
Add two lone pairs in axial (trans) positions
Observe the resulting square planar molecular geometry
Compare the predicted square planar structure to the experimentally observed structure of xenon tetrafluoride

scenes.brief_purpose: Synthesize all five electron-domain geometries and their lone-pair modifications into a unified framework; students match predictions to real molecular structures
key_visuals: Table or chart summarizing all five electron-domain geometries, their bond angles, and lone-pair effects
3D models of sample molecules: CH₄, H₂O, NH₃, CO₂, BF₃, SF₄, XeF₄, SF₆, PF₅
Side-by-side comparison of predicted (VSEPR) vs. observed structures
student_actions: Given a Lewis structure, determine electron-domain geometry, count lone pairs, and predict molecular geometry
Assess bond angles and explain deviations from idealized values
Match multiple molecules to their predicted VSEPR shapes
Reflect on how VSEPR successfully explains observed 3D structures across a range of real compounds
